yugadharma
(‘characteristics of the [four] युगस्’)
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् often mention the four yugas—Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali—which come and go in a cyclic order. They are actually epochs differing from one another in their characteristic features.
One of the simple, but nice, descriptions of such characteristics, called yuga-dharmas, is found in the Parāśarasamṛti (circa A.

). It may be briefly summarised as follows:
In the कृतयुग, तपस् or austerity was given the most important place in life. The Manusmṛti was the standard work, the rules of which were strictly followed. Since it was also called Satyayuga, people would leave the country itself if they saw sinful deeds committed anywhere. Even talking to a sinner was considered a sin. Curses uttered by the people—since they were extremely pious—would take effect immediately. Donors were so generous that they themselves would personally approach the needy and give them what they wanted.
In the त्रेतायुग there was slight deterioration in the standards of ethical life. ज्ञान or knowledge was considered all-important. The Gautamadharmasūtras was the standard text followed. People would desert their village itself if they saw sinful deeds committed. Even accidentally touching a sinner was itself considered a sin. A curse uttered against anyone would act within ten days. Generous donors would give gifts after calling or inviting the needy ones.
In the द्वापरयुग धर्म declined further, to the tune of fifty percent. यज्ञ (Vedic rituals) was the order of the day. The Śaṅkha-लिखित-dharmasūtras was the main authority for धर्म. If in any family धर्म was transgressed even by one, the whole family was abandoned. Anyone accepting ड़ोओद् from a sinner was deemed to have sinned himself. Curses uttered would take a month to become effective. Gifts used to be given after the person begged for it.
The कलियुग was deemed to be the worst. धर्म would have decreased to such an extent with only a quarter left behind. दान or giving gifts was the most important righteous act. The Parāśara Smṛti was the standard holy text to be followed. If a sin were committed by a person, only he had to be abandoned. Persons perpetrating sinful deeds were considered depraved. Curses would take a year to become effective. Gifts would be given only after extracting service.
In कलियुग, धर्म and सत्य (truth) would be overcome by अधर्म and अनृत (untruth). Servants would rule over kings and women over men. Religious rites like अग्निहोत्र would decline, honouring elders would disappear and young girls give birth to babies! Thus there would be an all-round decline of values.

yugādi
(‘beginning of an epoch’)
------------------------------------------
The arrival of the New Year is a great event that is duly celebrated by the people of all religions and cultures, all over the world. The most widely accepted New Year’s Day among the Hindus is the Cāndramāna युगादि, the first day of the bright half of the month of चैत्र (March-April). It is one of the 3½ days considered to be extremely auspicious, the others being विजयदशमी, बलिप्रतिपदा, and Akṣayyatṛtīyā. ब्रह्मा, the Creator, is said to have created this world on this day and the reckoning of time begun from the sunrise of this day. Hence the name ‘yugādi’ (beginning of an era or epoch). Emperor Śālīvāhana (circa A.

) is believed to have been crowned on this day. Consequently this era is called the Śaka Era or the Śālīvāhana Śaka.
Paścāttāpa or repentance for the evil deeds committed during the past year, (whether knowingly or unknowingly), prayers for forgiveness, performance of महाशान्ति rites to ward off all future evils or misfortune, worship of the presiding deity of the year as indicated by the day of the week on which the युगादि falls चन्द्र or the मोओन् is the king of that year.">1, worship of ब्रह्मा the Creator with all the उपचारस् (items showing honour), worship to other deities, to units of time and nakṣatras or asterisms and finally to Viṣṇu—are the religious rites specially recommended. ब्राह्मणस् of learning and good character have to be honoured on this day by feeding them with ड़ोओद् and offering gifts of money, water-pot and a copy of the new पञ्चाङ्ग (almanac). One should also listen to the reading of that पञ्चाङ्ग by the family priest.
Taking bath after anointing the body with oil (called ‘abhyañjanasnāna’ or ‘oil-bath’ in the Indian English), wearing new clothes, decorating the होउसे, eating a mixture of tender neem leaves and jaggery followed by a sumptuous feast, giving presents to servants and dependents—these are the social aspects of the celebration.
Listening to the forecasts given in the पञ्चाङ्ग can help one to prepare himself for facing the untoward incidents or circumstances. Eating the mixture of the bitter neem leaves along with the sweet jaggery is supposed to be good for health and also an antidote for the illnesses common in the spring season. Taken in a symbolic sense, it can psychologically prepare one to be equanimous under all circumstances of life, whether bringing pain or pleasure, since the new year may not be much different from the previous one!
Cāndramāna युगादि is observed widely as the New Year’s Day in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Maharashtra. In some parts of the country, especially in Maharashtra, a long bamboo is decorated with a silk cloth and a silver or copper vessel is put over it. A garland of sweets and neem leaves is tied at the upper end. This is called ‘guḍhi.’ This is then worshipped and hoisted on the terrace of the होउसे. It is taken down after sunset and the sweets and neem leaves are distributed among all, especially the children, to be consumed as prasāda or consecrated ड़ोओद्. Because of this custom of raising the guḍhi on the paḍhvā (or pratipad) day, the day (Yugādi) itself is christened as ‘Guḍhi Paḍvā.’ According to one belief, this is actually a flag-hoisting ceremony to commemorate the killing of Vālī, the monkey chief of किष्किन्धा, by Śrī राम on this day.
Yugādi is also the first day of the nine-day festival—Vasantanavarātra—dedicated to the worship of the Divine मोथेर् दुर्गा. Why there are two Navarātras, one in Vasanta ṛtu (spring) and the other in Śaradṛtu (autumn), is a matter of conjecture. It is possible that the two festivals became popular due to the fact of the spring crops and the autumn crops being ready at these times. However, celebration of the Vasantanavarātra has almost been given up in favour of Śarannavarātra.
The commencement of the New Year differs in some places. In Tamil Nadu and Kerala, following the solar चलेन्दर्, it starts generally on the 14th April (first day of the month Cittirai). In Bengal, it is ‘Pahalā Vaiśākh,’ falling mostly on the 15th of April. In other places like Gujarat it is on the Balipāḍyamī day (Kārttīka śukla pratipad).

Yugapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
This forms the 113th chapter of the treatise Gārgī Saṁhitā, a work on अस्त्रोलोग्य्. It is sometimes called Skanda-purāṇa—not to be confused with the well-known bigger work—probably because it begins with a question by स्कन्द to शिव. It is placed at 100 B. C.
Couched in the style of the पुराणस् it deals mainly with the characteristics of the four yugas—Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali—that of कलियुग resembling closely with the one given in the Vanaparva (Chapter 188, verses 30-64) of the epic Mahābhārata.
The attack on साकेत and Pāṭālīputra by the kings of Pāñcāla and मथुरा along with the यवनस् gets a prominent place. The depredations of the enemy armies and destruction of the civilian population make a dismal reading.

yugas
------------------------------------------
The concept of kāla or time as evolved by the Hindu scriptures from the smallest unit to colossal limits is, to say the least, मिन्द्-boggling.
Nimeṣa, the time taken for winking the eyelids once, is taken as the smallest unit.
The biggest unit, for the purpose of expounding the concept of yuga, can be taken as one day of ब्रह्मा, the four-faced creator. It is called कल्प. In terms of human years it is 4.32 billion (4.32 x 109) years.
This कल्प includes 1000 mahāyugas. Each mahāyuga—also called caturyuga—consists of the four well-known युगस्: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and कलि.
The following table gives an idea of these four युगस् in terms of divine and human years, the divine year being 360 times the human year:
Divine Years Human Years
Kṛtayuga 4800 17,28,000
Tretāyuga 3600 12,96,000
Dvāparayuga 2400 8,64,000
Kaliyuga 1200 4,32,000

Each of these युगस् is preceded by a short period called सन्ध्या and followed by another, called sandhyāṁśa.
Thus, the कृतयुग is preceded by 400 divine years (sandhyā) and followed by another 400 divine years (sandhyāṁśa). The figures for the other three are 300 + 300; 200 + 200; 100 + 100.
The descriptions given so far are based on the ones commonly found in the epics and the पुराणस् (vide Viṣṇupurāṇa 1.3; 6.3).
However, the meaning and concept seem to have undergone quite a few changes in course of time. In the Vedāṅgajyautiṣa (verse 5) it is a duration of five years. In the Ṛgveda (3.26.3) it means just a day or a very short period. In other places, the names Kṛta and so on have been used to indicate a number got by the throw of dice. (vide Chāndogya Upaniṣad

.)
See also DVĀPARAYUGA, KĀLA, KALIYUGA, KALPA, KṚTAYUGA, MANVANTARA, TRETĀYUGA.
